title: Restricted arrangements and neighbour rules
transcript: An arrangement depends on order. When two named objects must stay next to each other, treat them as one movable block first. Once you place the block, restore the allowed orders inside it. That internal choice is part of the count.

In AMC practice, neighbour rules may appear in seating plans, passwords, queues or objects on a shelf. Start with the rule that restricts the most. Rossmoyne style counting can combine two neighbour conditions. A block count and an overlap check prevent double counting.
Line up three distinct keys named A, B and C. How many different orders can you make? Keep track of which objects are still free after you choose the first one.

There are three choices for the first position. Each first choice leaves two for the second and then one for the last. Multiply three times two times one. Each full set of choices produces a different line. There are six orders.
There are six distinct keys in a row. A and B must be adjacent. How many arrangements are possible? A might sit before or after B. Take both possibilities into account.

Compress A and B into one block. Now there are just five objects to arrange. Those objects can be ordered in one hundred and twenty ways. In each arrangement the pair can be A B or B A. Multiply by two, giving two hundred and forty original arrangements. The block can be identified in each one.

Line up seven distinct keys, including A, B, C and D. Consider two pairs: A with B, and C with D. How many orders leave both of those pairs nonadjacent? Draw the two possible adjacency conditions as overlapping sets.

There are five thousand and forty total orders. The number making A and B adjacent is twice seven hundred and twenty, or one thousand four hundred and forty. The other pair has the same count. If both pairs are adjacent, arrange five objects with two blocks. Each block has two internal orders, giving four hundred and eighty shared arrangements. The shared arrangements have been counted in both single-pair totals. Decide whether you need to remove the overlap once or twice.

The number with at least one pair adjacent is the two individual counts minus the shared four hundred and eighty. Remove those from the grand total. The answer is two thousand six hundred and forty. Check that your accepted arrangements satisfy the exact condition about how many adjacent pairs there are.

When a required adjacent pair is one block, count both internal orders if the problem allows them. The block is still a group of two distinct objects. A pair that is forbidden to sit together is often easiest to count as a complement. The overlap of two forbidden conditions can be counted twice.

Mark whether order matters. For a required pair, draw a bracket around the neighbours and count what can move. Work out the order inside each block. For multiple restrictions, choose disjoint cases or show the overlap explicitly.
